results.name: pair_out_of_span_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets outside the span of two-example sets (strictly below the smaller or above the larger example); observed below null_mean means the model over-generalizes beyond a pair of examples.
results.code:
# name: pair_out_of_span_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets outside the span of two-example sets (strictly below the smaller or above the larger example); observed below null_mean means the model over-generalizes beyond a pair of examples.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    out = (t < np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) | (t > np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    m = (n == 2) & out
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: yes_rate_decline_over_session
results.description: Yes-rate in the first third of each session (trial_index < 150) minus the last third (trial_index >= 300); observed above null_mean means people grow more conservative over the session than the time-invariant model predicts from the stimuli alone.

results.name: singleton_near_minus_far_gradient
results.description: For one-example sets and targets other than the example, yes-rate when |target - example| <= 10 minus when it is > 10; observed above null_mean means people show a steeper magnitude-similarity gradient around a single example than the model's interval hypotheses produce (below means shallower).
results.code:
# name: singleton_near_minus_far_gradient
# description: For one-example sets and targets other than the example, yes-rate when |target - example| <= 10 minus when it is > 10; observed above null_mean means people show a steeper magnitude-similarity gradient around a single example than the model's interval hypotheses produce (below means shallower).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "nan"), errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d = np.abs(t - x)
    ok = single.to_numpy() & (d > 0)
    near = ok & (d <= 10)
    far = ok & (d > 10)
    if not near.any() or not far.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: pure_parity_inspan_match_minus_mismatch
results.description: In 2+-example sets whose examples all share one parity, yes-rate for same-parity non-example targets inside the span minus opposite-parity targets inside the span; observed above null_mean means the parity penalty for in-range targets is larger than the model's constant veto plus inferred concept produce (below means smaller).
results.code:
# name: pure_parity_inspan_match_minus_mismatch
# description: In 2+-example sets whose examples all share one parity, yes-rate for same-parity non-example targets inside the span minus opposite-parity targets inside the span; observed above null_mean means the parity penalty for in-range targets is larger than the model's constant veto plus inferred concept produce (below means smaller).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    odd = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 2) == 1, False).sum(axis=1)
    pure = (n >= 2) & ((odd == 0) | (odd == n))
    par = np.mod(np.nan_to_num(ex[:, 0]), 2)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    inset = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    inspan = (t >= np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) & (t <= np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    same = np.mod(t, 2) == par
    base = pure & inspan & ~inset
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a, b = base & same, base & ~same
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: mixed_parity_large_set_inspan_yes
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets inside the examples' span in 3-4-example sets whose examples include both odd and even numbers; observed above null_mean means people fill in the range of heterogeneous sets more readily than the model (which keeps posterior mass on sparse rules).
results.code:
# name: mixed_parity_large_set_inspan_yes
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets inside the examples' span in 3-4-example sets whose examples include both odd and even numbers; observed above null_mean means people fill in the range of heterogeneous sets more readily than the model (which keeps posterior mass on sparse rules).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    odd = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 2) == 1, False).sum(axis=1)
    mixed = (odd > 0) & (odd < n)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    inset = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    inspan = (t >= np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)) & (t <= np.nanmax(ex, axis=1))
    m = (n >= 3) & mixed & inspan & ~inset
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: upward_minus_downward_extension
results.description: Among multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets above the largest example minus yes-rate for targets below the smallest example; observed different from null_mean means people extend the concept asymmetrically in magnitude (above = more upward generalization) beyond what the model's symmetric intervals and rules imply.
results.code:
# name: upward_minus_downward_extension
# description: Among multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets above the largest example minus yes-rate for targets below the smallest example; observed different from null_mean means people extend the concept asymmetrically in magnitude (above = more upward generalization) beyond what the model's symmetric intervals and rules imply.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    up = (n >= 2) & (t > mx)
    down = (n >= 2) & (t < mn)
    if not up.any() or not down.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[down].mean())

results.name: example_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null_mean means the model over-endorses the examples (it treats them as near-certain members while people say no to them ~14% of the time).
results.code:
# name: example_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null_mean means the model over-endorses the examples (it treats them as near-certain members while people say no to them ~14% of the time).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()[:, None]
    inset = (ex.to_numpy() == t).any(axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    return float(r[inset].mean()) if inset.any() else 0.0

results.name: between_participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across participants (a new participant starts each time trial_index resets to 0 in row order) of each participant's overall yes-rate; observed above null_mean means people differ in yes-bias more than the single-population model allows.
results.code:
# name: between_participant_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across participants (a new participant starts each time trial_index resets to 0 in row order) of each participant's overall yes-rate; observed above null_mean means people differ in yes-bias more than the single-population model allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    pid = np.cumsum(np.r_[True, ti[1:] <= ti[:-1]])
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    means = pd.Series(r).groupby(pid).mean().to_numpy()
    return float(np.std(means)) if len(means) > 1 else 0.0
